summary: The note explains how After-Action Reviews (AARs) help emergency management agencies learn from crises, using the September 15, 2024 East Coast power and internet outage as a case study. Lessons include flexible protocols, resilient technology, community education, cross-agency collaboration, and proactive drills. The overall argument is that AARs drive continuous improvement and a more resilient future.
one_line: After-Action Reviews of the September 15, 2024 East Coast outage show how agencies improve emergency preparedness through flexibility, technology, education, collaboration and drills.
key_facts: After-Action Reviews (AARs) are debriefs in which participants from every level of a response examine what occurred, why it happened, and how it can be done better.
Jack Thompson, Director of the Regional Emergency Response Team, said AARs "are not just a checkbox exercise."
AAR scope has expanded beyond tangible outcomes like speed of service restoration to intangibles such as communication efficacy and team coordination.
Nancy Langford, an emergency management consultant, said reviews now look at leaders' emotional intelligence, staff stress levels, and how information circulated among the public.
The East Coast power and internet outage of September 15, 2024 was caused by a compound of natural events and mechanical failings and led to a 72-hour service interruption affecting millions.
The AAR of the September outage was led by experts including Nancy Langford and Jack Thompson.
A key finding was the need for flexibility in protocols; Thompson said "plans are the starting point, not the playbook."
Dr. Adam Richmond, a technology analyst, said mesh networks and mobile communication apps can be lifesaving when standard systems fail.

Agencies are adopting technologies less susceptible to single points of failure and accelerating deployment of mobile solar-powered charging stations and emergency messaging that does not depend on the internet.
Samantha Kline, a community outreach coordinator, observed that well-educated, engaged communities fared better after the outage.
Programs now include bolstering neighborhood watch programs and holding regular town hall meetings on preparedness.
Lieutenant Tyler Harrison of the state police said interagency communication "has never been better" after the September outage.
Agencies are shifting to anticipatory preparedness with mock drills and proactive assessments; Dr. Leslie Tam heads a regional preparedness consortium.
